title: Lucena and Philidor: the two rook endings to know
outcomes: Explains in plain words how the attacker wins with a pawn on the seventh (Lucena) and how the defender draws with the rook on the sixth rank (Philidor)

steps.text: Two rook endings to know. In **Lucena** the pawn stands on the seventh, your king is in front of it and the enemy king is cut off; you win by getting the king out of the way of checks. In **Philidor** the defender keeps the rook on the sixth rank and checks from behind once the pawn advances. Both are plans with conditions.

steps.text: **Conditions.** Lucena needs a pawn on the seventh, your king in front and the enemy king cut off. Promoting at once, or blocking a check with a loose rook, throws the win away. **Philidor** is a plan: a rook on the sixth rank is a good default, not the only drawing idea. Its check from behind fails if White's rook can capture it.

steps.text: Can a lone king catch a runaway pawn? Count the pawn's steps to the eighth rank and draw a square with that many squares on a side, starting at the pawn. If the defending king is inside the square, or steps into it on his move, he catches the pawn. This **rule of the square** is a heuristic: it counts only the pawn and the defending king.

title: Which squares does a piece attack?
outcomes: Taps every square a rook, bishop, knight or pawn attacks when other pieces stand in the way
Stops a line at the first piece it meets and keeps the squares behind it out
Knows a pawn attacks diagonally ahead, even when blocked, and not straight ahead
Says a defended piece is still attacked

steps.text:
A piece **attacks** a square when it could capture an enemy piece standing there (pins aside; see the next card). If the square holds a piece of its own side, we say the piece **defends** it.
An attacked square need not hold anything yet. And the squares a piece attacks are not always the squares it moves to.

steps.text:
A check before you trust 'attacks'.
**Lines:** a rook, bishop or queen attacks up to and including the first piece it meets. Squares behind it are not attacked until it leaves.
**Pawns:** two squares diagonally ahead, even when blocked; never the square straight ahead.
**Pinned pieces** still attack their squares. A defended piece is still attacked.

steps.text: **En passant** means 'in passing'. When an enemy pawn jumps two squares and lands right beside your pawn, you may capture it as if it had moved only one square. You must do it on the very next move, or the chance is gone.

A game is a **draw** when: a player has no legal move and is not in check (stalemate); the same position occurs three times (repetition); fifty moves pass without a capture or a pawn move; there are not enough pieces to checkmate; or both players agree. Do not assume that an extra piece always wins.

steps.text:
The **safety scan** is the two questions from the threat lesson, run on every move in about ten seconds.
**1. What did my opponent's last move threaten or open?**
**2. Is any of my pieces loose, or attacked by something cheaper?**
This is a habit to try, not a law. It catches obvious dangers, not deep ones.

Ask: **is it attacked, and what would the trade cost me?**
The scan also works the other way. Your opponent's loose pieces are chances.

title: Candidates and short lines

steps.text: Do not play the first good-looking move. Make a short **candidate list**: two to four moves, forcing moves first. Then follow each for about three **plies** (a ply is one move by one side): your move, the opponent's best reply, your next move. Drop candidates that clearly fail. Two to four is a habit to try, not a rule.

steps.text: To follow a line you must hold the board in your head. **Drill:** you study a position for 15 seconds, then some pieces vanish from the board. You must still say where a piece can go. This is a training exercise for seeing lines, not a chess rule.

**Short lines have limits.** Three plies are enough when every move is forcing. They can mislead when a sacrifice pays off later: a line that looks bad at ply three can be mate at ply five. And in quiet positions the candidates may not separate at all.
Ask: **is the last move of my line quiet or forcing?**

title: How deep? Spend calculation where it pays
outcomes: Follows a forcing line to a quiet position before judging it
Tells critical moments from routine ones
Gives reasons to stop a line
Records how deep a line went and whether it was worth it

steps.text:
Depth is a **budget**, not a virtue. Habits to try:
**Go deep** when every move in the line is a check, capture or threat: the replies are few.
**Stop** when the position is quiet and you can compare it, when you have found a refutation, or when the clock says so.
**Spend more** at critical moments, less at routine ones.

The king must take.

The bishop blocks.

claims.statement: Rxh7+ forces checkmate in three.
Rxh7+ is the engine's best move.

steps.text:

steps.text: Two steps, in this order. **Eliminate:** for each candidate, look for one concrete reply that refutes it: a capture, a check, a threat. steps.text:
An open file is a road, not a prize. A rook standing on it does nothing until it can **land** on a square in the enemy camp, best of all on the seventh rank, where pawns and the king are cramped.

**The entry square is not guarded by a pawn or a minor piece.**
**Something is waiting there:** undefended pawns, or a king with no room.

**Can a pawn of his protect it?**
**Can my pieces reach it,** for example along an open file?
**Do I attack it more often than he defends it?**
A pawn that fails these tests is just a pawn.

steps.text: A **time budget** is a plan for where the clock goes: a share for each phase, a reserve for the end, and room to think longer on the few moves that matter. **The same time on every move is not a budget**: it pays as much for a forced reply as for a decision. Every number here is a first guess to test against your own clock.

Forced replies cost almost nothing. The prices (10 seconds, one minute) are a rule of thumb to adjust, not a measured optimum.

steps.text:
Before you capture on a square, **count**. List every piece that can capture there for each side, with its value. The side that starts captures with its **cheapest** piece first, and either side may stop whenever carrying on would lose material.
Then compare: what do I win, and what do I lose?

**The arrival is effective.** Not boxed in, and not attacked on its landing square by a piece of lower counting value.

steps.text:
When one of your pieces is attacked and nothing defends it, you have five kinds of answer.
**Move** it. **Defend** it. **Capture** the attacker. **Block** the line (only against a bishop, rook or queen). **Counterattack** with a bigger threat of your own.
List them before you choose. A counterattack works only if your threat is bigger than theirs, so as a rule of thumb look at the first four first.

An answer must pass two checks.
**Does it stop the attack?** A defender fails when the attacker has a lower counting value (a rule of thumb): a pawn takes a defended knight and you only win the pawn back. A move far from both pieces does nothing unless it makes a bigger threat.
**Does it leave something else loose?** A defender that moves can leave the piece it guarded loose.

title: Real threats and fictitious ones

An attacked piece is not always in danger. A threat is **real** if the capture gains something against best defence. It is **fictitious** if the capture fails. Three common reasons: the piece is defended and the attacker has a higher counting value; the attacker is **pinned to its king** and may not capture; the capture would let you win something bigger.

The other mistake is spending a move on a threat that is not there. **Rule of thumb:** check the capture first; react only if it works.

title: Perpetual check: the draw you can force

steps.text: A **perpetual check** is a series of checks that the king cannot escape, so the same position keeps returning. When a position occurs three times, a player can claim a draw (see *L-FND-SPECIAL-1*). When you are worse, a perpetual can save half a point. It works only if the king has nowhere to hide, so **test the king's squares** before you rely on it.

line.say: The queen takes a pawn with check. The king has only one legal move.

Forced. The queen can go back to f7.
The position after the first check is back, for the second time. A third time allows a draw claim.

No black piece attacks the queen on f7.
After Qxf7+ Kh8 Qf8+ the king on h8 again has exactly one legal move (h7).
After five moves the queen is on f7 again.
And the black king is on h7 again.

steps.text:
Three tests before you rely on a perpetual.
**Where can the king go?** Count its flight squares after each check.
**Can the checker be captured, or the check blocked?**
**Is the draw really your best result?** If another move wins, or the perpetual is not there, a draw may be a mistake. *Rule of thumb:* take the perpetual only when the alternatives are worse.

title: Pins: cannot move, or should not move

steps.text:
A **pin** attacks a piece that cannot, or should not, move, because a more valuable piece stands behind it on the same line.
In an **absolute** pin the piece behind is the king, so moving the pinned piece is illegal. A pinned piece is easy prey: it cannot run away from a second attacker.

steps.text:
Two kinds of pin.
**Absolute:** the king is behind. The pinned piece has no legal move.
**Relative:** something valuable, but not the king, is behind. The piece may legally move, but then it loses what stood behind it.
'Cannot move' and 'should not move' differ. A **fork** is one piece attacking two targets; a pin needs a line with something behind.

steps.text: Some pins win nothing at once. A pinned piece stays tied to its square and is a poor defender, which can shape play for many moves. Whether that matters is judged case by case, and later strategy lessons return to it.

title: In-between moves: a check or capture first
outcomes: Asks, before a capture or recapture, whether a check or capture can be played first

steps.text:
An **in-between move** (German: *Zwischenzug*) is a forcing move you play *before* the reply your opponent expects, such as the recapture. It is usually a **check**, which the opponent must answer, or a **capture**.
The question to ask before any capture or recapture: **is there a check or capture I can play first, and does my original capture still work afterwards?**

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn on c3 attacks the rook on d4, and Black's bishop on a6 attacks the white rook on b5. The expected move is to take on d4.

line.say: The attacked rook moves with check along the c-file. Black has to answer the check first.
The king steps aside. The white rook has left b5, so the bishop can no longer take it there.
Now the pawn takes the rook on d4. Along the engine line White gains at least five points of material.

claims.statement: The engine's best move is Rc5+ (depth 16).
Along the engine line White gains at least five points of material.
Taking at once with cxd4 is at least 600 centipawns worse (engine).
Black's bishop on a6 attacks the rook on b5.
The pawn on c3 attacks the rook on d4.

steps.text:
**When it works:** the in-between move forces a reply, and afterwards the capture you wanted still wins what you expected. **Rule of thumb:** look at checks first, because the reply is forced.
**When it fails:** for example when a pawn defends the target, so the follow-up capture wins nothing. After the forcing move, count the exchange again, and ask whether the opponent has an in-between move of their own.
